name: Pontine arteries
summary: Numerous small branches leave the basilar artery along its course and enter the pons. The paramedian arteries pierce the ventral pons beside the midline and supply the corticospinal fibers, pontine nuclei, medial lemniscus and the abducens and facial nuclei; the short circumferential branches supply the anterolateral pons and the long circumferential branches (AICA, SCA) the lateral tegmentum. Paramedian branch disease from basilar atheroma is a very common cause of pontine lacunes.

anatomy.location: Arise from the posterior and lateral walls of the basilar artery in the prepontine cistern and enter the basilar sulcus and anterolateral surface of the pons; they do not anastomose significantly with one another.

subdivisions.name: Paramedian arteries
subdivisions.note: medial basis pontis and medial tegmentum: corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers, pontine nuclei, medial lemniscus, abducens nucleus, facial nucleus, MLF

subdivisions.name: Short circumferential arteries
subdivisions.note: anterolateral basis pontis and middle cerebellar peduncle entry zone

subdivisions.name: Long circumferential arteries
subdivisions.note: lateral tegmentum, together with AICA and SCA branches

function: Supply the pons segment by segment: the corticospinal tract in the basis pontis, the pontine nuclei and transverse fibers, the medial lemniscus, the abducens and facial nuclei, the paramedian pontine reticular formation and the MLF.

bestView.label: paramedian basis pontis, the lacunar site
basilar artery on the ventral pons with perforators entering

imaging.normalAppearance: Individual perforators are not resolved on MRI. Their territories are the paramedian wedges of the pons on axial slices, best judged relative to the midline and the ventral surface.

pathology.finding: A wedge of restricted diffusion in one half of the basis pontis extending to the ventral surface (branch atheromatous disease) or a smaller deep lacune; the corticospinal tract is usually involved.
pathology.pitfalls: Pontine infarcts may not be visible on CT at all; DWI is essential

pathology.finding: A hyperdense hematoma centered in the pons, often extending into the fourth ventricle; large hemorrhages cause coma with pinpoint pupils.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI; CTA of the basilar artery for atheroma or occlusion

lesionEffects.mechanism: Corticospinal fibers in the basis pontis
Basis pontis at the level of the facial and hypoglossal projections

lesionEffects.deficit: Abducens palsy or horizontal gaze palsy with contralateral hemiparesis
lesionEffects.mechanism: Abducens nucleus/PPRF plus the corticospinal tract (Foville)
Facial fascicle plus the corticospinal tract (Millard–Gubler)

examination: Pronator drift and gait; check for ataxia out of proportion to weakness
Horizontal eye movements looking for adduction lag or gaze palsy
pearls: Lacunar syndromes come from the pons as often as from the internal capsule; ataxic hemiparesis and dysarthria–clumsy hand favor the pons
A crossed sign (cranial nerve on one side, limbs on the other) means the brainstem: pons if it is VI or VII
